key_points.point: The document emphasizes that risk management should be integrated into the AI lifecycle through standardized documentation and testing. By focusing on observable metrics and clear documentation of model behavior, organizations can maintain agility while ensuring safety. This aligns with the accelerationist view that safety is best achieved through empirical rigor and systematic oversight rather than restrictive, pre-deployment barriers.
key_points.verbatim: Standardized documentation can help organizations systematically integrate AI risk management processes and enhance accountability efforts. ... Documentation may generate downstream benefits related to improved system replicability and robustness.

key_points.point: The document encourages organizations to maintain comprehensive AI system inventories to enable quick resolution of queries regarding model performance and deployment status. By treating AI as a manageable asset within a structured database, organizations can improve operational efficiency and maintain a holistic view of their AI portfolio. This aligns with accelerationist goals of scaling AI deployment by reducing the friction associated with managing large-scale, complex AI systems.
key_points.verbatim: A serviceable AI system inventory may allow for the quick resolution of: specific queries for single models, such as 'when was this model last refreshed?' high-level queries across all models, such as, 'how many models are currently deployed within our organization?' or 'how many users are impacted by our models?'

key_points.point: The document emphasizes that AI systems should be evaluated based on their real-world performance and observable outcomes rather than just theoretical design. By focusing on iterative testing and monitoring, organizations can ensure safety through empirical evidence. This aligns with the accelerationist preference for learning by doing and continuous improvement over static, pre-deployment restrictions.
key_points.verbatim: Organizational policies and practices are in place to foster a critical thinking and safety-first mindset in the design, development, deployment, and uses of AI systems to minimize negative impacts.

key_points.point: The document supports the integration of AI into organizational decision-making and risk management frameworks. By leveraging AI for monitoring and governance, organizations can enhance their institutional resilience and operational adaptability. This aligns with the accelerationist goal of using AI to improve administrative and societal decision-making processes.
key_points.verbatim: Organizations can develop risk response plans based on strategies such as accepted model risk management, enterprise risk management, and information sharing and disclosure practices.

key_points.point: The document emphasizes that organizations should focus on measurable activities and continuous improvement to ensure AI systems remain performant and trustworthy. By integrating feedback loops and monitoring performance against trustworthiness characteristics, organizations can iterate on AI systems to enhance their utility and safety. This aligns with the accelerationist view that safety is best achieved through empirical, real-world testing and iterative refinement rather than pre-emptive, restrictive regulation.
key_points.verbatim: Measurable activities for continual improvements are integrated into AI system updates and include regular engagement with interested parties, including relevant AI actors.

key_points.point: The document supports the use of AI to improve quality of life and economic prosperity. It encourages organizations to document the potential positive impacts and benefits of AI systems. This aligns with the accelerationist goal of leveraging AI as a force for progress and solving human problems.
key_points.verbatim: AI systems have enormous potential to improve quality of life, enhance economic prosperity and security costs. Organizations are encouraged to define and document system purpose and utility, and its potential positive impacts and benefits beyond current known performance benchmarks.

key_points.point: The document argues that documentation is a critical component of accountability and risk management. It suggests that without clear records of AI actors, assumptions, and training data, organizations cannot effectively manage risks or respond to incidents. This supports the safetyist goal of creating transparent, auditable AI development processes to prevent catastrophic failures.
key_points.verbatim: Clear policies and procedures relating to documentation and transparency facilitate and enhance efforts to communicate roles and responsibilities for the Map, Measure and Manage functions across the AI lifecycle.

key_points.point: The document advocates for establishing formal governance frameworks that align AI systems with organizational values and legal standards. It emphasizes that risk management must be proactive, using impact assessments to prevent harm by design. This aligns with the safetyist desire to embed safety and ethical considerations into the foundational architecture of AI development.
key_points.verbatim: All stakeholders benefit from policies, processes, and procedures which require preventing harm by design and default.

key_points.point: The document emphasizes the necessity of clear human accountability frameworks, requiring organizations to define who is responsible for AI decisions and outcomes. It advocates for separating development and testing functions to prevent groupthink and ensure independent oversight. This approach seeks to mitigate catastrophic risks by embedding human-in-the-loop governance throughout the AI lifecycle.
key_points.verbatim: The development of a risk-aware organizational culture starts with defining responsibilities. For example, under some risk management structures, professionals carrying out test and evaluation tasks are independent from AI system developers and report through risk management functions or directly to executives.

key_points.point: The document proposes rigorous incident response and 'appeal and override' processes to manage autonomous AI agents. By establishing these mechanisms, organizations can flag potential incidents in real-time and provide human adjudication for system outcomes, which is critical for maintaining control over agentic infrastructure.
key_points.verbatim: Incident response and 'appeal and override' are commonly used processes in information technology management. These processes enable real-time flagging of potential incidents, and human adjudication of system outcomes.

key_points.point: The document mandates extensive documentation of AI systems, including data dictionaries, source code links, and incident response plans. This addresses the 'documentation debt' problem by ensuring that organizations have the necessary artifacts to maintain safety and transparency throughout the system's lifecycle.
key_points.verbatim: An AI system inventory is an organized database of artifacts relating to an AI system or model. It may include system documentation, incident response plans, data dictionaries, links to implementation software or source code, names and contact information for relevant AI actors.

key_points.point: The document promotes 'effective challenge' as a core cultural practice to prevent groupthink and identify design flaws. By empowering experts to question implementation decisions, organizations can proactively mitigate risks. This reflects the safetyist commitment to rigorous peer review and internal accountability structures.
key_points.verbatim: For example, 'effective challenge,' is a culture- based practice that encourages critical thinking and questioning of important design and implementation decisions by experts with the authority and stature to make such changes.

key_points.point: The document advocates for a 'three lines of defense' model to manage AI risks, ensuring that development, risk management, and auditing are handled by separate, accountable teams. This layered approach is designed to prevent single points of failure. It aligns with the safetyist preference for defense-in-depth strategies.
key_points.verbatim: Organizations in some industries implement three (or more) 'lines of defense,' where separate teams are held accountable for different aspects of the system lifecycle, such as development, risk management, and auditing.

key_points.point: Red-teaming is presented as a critical method for stress-testing AI systems to uncover vulnerabilities before they cause harm. By using independent experts to simulate adversarial conditions, organizations can identify failure modes. This is a core safetyist practice for proactive risk mitigation.
key_points.verbatim: Red-teaming is another risk measurement and management approach. This practice consists of adversarial testing of AI systems under stress conditions to seek out failure modes or vulnerabilities in the system.

key_points.point: The document emphasizes the need for clear human accountability for AI decisions, including who is responsible for maintenance and ethical considerations. This ensures that AI systems do not operate in a vacuum of responsibility. It aligns with the safetyist goal of maintaining human oversight over autonomous systems.
key_points.verbatim: Who is ultimately responsible for the decisions of the AI and is this person aware of the intended uses and limitations of the analytic?

key_points.point: The document advocates for a layered, defense-in-depth approach to AI risk management. It emphasizes the need for continuous monitoring, contingency planning, and the ability to deactivate systems that exceed risk tolerances. This strategy ensures that single points of failure or emergent risks do not lead to catastrophic outcomes.
key_points.verbatim: Organizations are encouraged to establish risk management protocols with consideration of the trustworthiness characteristics, the deployment context, and real world impacts.

key_points.point: The document mandates clear assignment of human responsibility for AI systems throughout their lifecycle. It requires organizations to document roles, authorities, and accountability for maintenance and decommissioning. This ensures that human oversight remains central to AI governance.
key_points.verbatim: What are the roles, responsibilities, and delegation of authorities of personnel involved in the design, development, deployment, assessment and monitoring of the AI system?

key_points.point: The document promotes a holistic governance framework that addresses system-wide architecture rather than just individual model performance. It calls for integrating interdisciplinary teams and external expertise to manage risks associated with complex, adaptive systems.
key_points.verbatim: Organizational risk response may entail identifying and analyzing alternative approaches, methods, processes or systems, and balancing tradeoffs between trustworthiness characteristics and how they relate to organizational principles and societal values.

key_points.point: The document advocates for a comprehensive governance framework that requires organizations to document third-party dependencies, monitor performance, and establish clear accountability structures. It promotes a 'go/no-go' decision-making process based on risk tolerance, ensuring that systems are only deployed if they meet safety and ethical standards. This reflects the safetyist priority of establishing systemic oversight before and during deployment.
key_points.verbatim: Focusing first and foremost on risks involving physical safety, legal liabilities, regulatory compliance, and negative impacts on individuals, groups, or society is recommended.

key_points.point: The document recognizes that relying on third-party components, such as pre-trained models, introduces significant systemic risk due to increased complexity and opacity. It notes that these dependencies make it difficult to anticipate negative outcomes or perform root cause analyses, necessitating rigorous monitoring and documentation of data provenance.
key_points.verbatim: The use of pre-trained models can make it difficult to anticipate negative system outcomes or impacts. Lack of documentation or transparency tools increases the difficulty and general complexity when deploying pre-trained models and hinders root cause analyses.

key_points.point: The document mandates that organizations establish testing and evaluation processes that prioritize transparency. It specifically calls for documentation of data provenance, model limitations, and the rationale behind system design to ensure that AI systems are explainable and accountable to stakeholders.
key_points.verbatim: Establish testing, evaluation, validation and verification processes for third-party AI systems which address the needs for transparency without exposing proprietary algorithms.

key_points.point: The document argues that AI risks are inherently socio-technical, arising from the interaction between technical design and social context. It advocates for a holistic governance approach that moves beyond isolated technical metrics to consider the entire system lifecycle. This aligns with the safetyist view that AI cannot be treated as a standalone artifact but must be managed as a complex, embedded system.
key_points.verbatim: Socio-technical AI risks emerge from the interplay between technical development decisions and how a system is used, who operates it, and the social context into which it is deployed. Addressing these risks is complex and requires a commitment to understanding how contextual factors may interact with AI lifecycle actions.

key_points.point: The document emphasizes the need for formal human-AI accountability frameworks, specifically regarding 'go/no-go' deployment decisions. It argues that these decisions must remain independent of financial or reputational interests, reflecting a safetyist concern that corporate incentives often undermine safety. It suggests that if risk mapping is too difficult, organizations should default to a 'no-go' decision.
key_points.verbatim: Go/no-go decisions related to AI system risks can take stakeholder feedback into account, but remain independent from stakeholdersâ€™ vested financial or reputational interests. If mapping risk is prohibitively difficult, a "no-go" decision may be considered for the specific system.

key_points.point: The document warns that AI development often suffers from 'documentation debt' and a narrow focus on computational requirements, which leads to the neglect of stakeholder needs and human values. It asserts that without proactive, interdisciplinary requirements elicitation, organizations will over-rely on implicit biases and groupthink, undermining the trustworthiness of the system.
key_points.verbatim: When written requirements are unavailable or incomplete, AI actors may inadvertently overlook business and stakeholder needs, over-rely on implicit human biases such as confirmation bias and groupthink, and maintain exclusive focus on computational requirements.

key_points.point: The document emphasizes the necessity of human oversight in AI systems, particularly as they move from decision support to automated decision-making. It argues that oversight is a shared responsibility requiring organizational buy-in and accountability mechanisms. This reflects the safetyist focus on maintaining human control over autonomous systems.
key_points.verbatim: Defining and differentiating various human roles and responsibilities for AI systemsâ€™ governance, and differentiating AI system overseers and those using or interacting with AI systems can enhance AI risk management activities. In critical systems, high-stakes settings, and systems deemed high-risk it is of vital importance to evaluate risks and effectiveness of oversight procedures before an AI system is deployed.

key_points.point: The document advocates for a layered approach to risk management, including red teaming, impact assessment, and the use of TEVV (Test, Evaluation, Verification, and Validation) resources. It suggests that organizations should identify and document the likelihood and magnitude of both benefits and harms. This aligns with the safetyist preference for defense-in-depth and proactive risk mitigation.
key_points.verbatim: Establish processes for red teaming to identify and connect system limitations to AI lifecycle stage(s) and potential downstream impacts. Apply TEVV regularly at key stages in the AI lifecycle, connected to system impacts and frequency of system updates.

key_points.point: The document advocates for a socio-technical approach to AI governance, emphasizing that AI systems are not just technical artifacts but are embedded in complex social and human contexts. It argues that effective risk management requires evaluating the entire system architecture, including human operators and the social environment, rather than focusing solely on model performance. This aligns with the safetyist goal of governing the broader system to prevent unforeseen societal harms.
key_points.verbatim: AI systems are socio-technical in nature and can have positive, neutral, or negative implications that extend beyond their stated purpose. Negative impacts can be wideranging and affect individuals, groups, communities, organizations, and society, as well as the environment and national security.

key_points.point: The document mandates that organizations document their AI systems' internal reasoning, performance metrics, and testing methodologies to ensure transparency. By requiring organizations to explain how they manage potential biases and unfair outcomes, it forces AI systems to 'show their work' to stakeholders and regulators. This transparency is presented as a foundational requirement for building trustworthy AI.
key_points.verbatim: If the AI system relates to people, does it unfairly advantage or disadvantage a particular social group? In what ways? How was this managed?

key_points.point: The document emphasizes the necessity of maintaining human oversight throughout the AI lifecycle, specifically by involving independent assessors and domain experts who are separate from the front-line development team. It argues that relying on local evaluations is insufficient, and that continuous monitoring by diverse, interdisciplinary teams is required to identify 'pockets of failures' that standard metrics might miss. This strategy aims to ensure that human judgment remains central to AI assurance.
key_points.verbatim: Involving internal experts who did not serve as front-line developers for the system and/or independent assessors regular assessments of AI systems helps a fulsome characterization of AI systems’ performance and trustworthiness.

key_points.point: The document advocates for using AI to monitor AI, specifically through real-time performance tracking and anomaly detection. This approach aims to identify drift and failures that occur when systems operate outside their design assumptions. By implementing automated alerts and human-in-the-loop oversight, organizations can mitigate risks associated with autonomous system behavior.
key_points.verbatim: Monitor for anomalies using approaches such as control limits, confidence intervals, integrity constraints and ML algorithms. When anomalies are observed, consider error propagation and feedback loop risks.

key_points.point: The document emphasizes the necessity of explainability and interpretability to ensure system trustworthiness. It distinguishes between transparency (what happened), explainability (how a decision was made), and interpretability (why a decision was made). These mechanisms are presented as essential tools for debugging, auditing, and enabling human recourse for problematic AI outcomes.
key_points.verbatim: Transparency, explainability, and interpretability are distinct characteristics that support each other. Transparency can answer the question of “what happened”. Explainability can answer the question of “how” a decision was made in the system. Interpretability can answer the question of “why” a decision was made by the system and its meaning or context to the user.

key_points.point: The document promotes a defense-in-depth strategy for AI security, including red-teaming, watermarking, and incident response planning. It argues that security and resilience are distinct but related, requiring proactive protection against adversarial attacks and the ability to degrade gracefully during failures. This framework treats AI systems as critical infrastructure that must be hardened against exploitation.
key_points.verbatim: While resilience is the ability to return to normal function after an unexpected adverse event, security includes resilience but also encompasses protocols to avoid, protect against, respond to, or recover from attacks.

key_points.point: The document emphasizes that organizations must document the level of explainability required for AI determinations and the intervals for checking accuracy and bias. This reflects a safetyist commitment to transparency as a prerequisite for accountability. By mandating documentation of data provenance and system limitations, the playbook aims to prevent opaque decision-making processes that could lead to catastrophic or systemic failures.
key_points.verbatim: Given the purpose of the AI, what level of explainability or interpretability is required for how the AI made its determination? How has the entity documented the AI system’s data provenance, including sources, origins, transformations, augmentations, labels, dependencies, constraints, and metadata?

key_points.point: The document asserts that AI systems can introduce new privacy risks by allowing inferences that identify individuals or reveal previously private information. It highlights that privacy-related risks are interconnected with security, bias, and transparency, necessitating a holistic risk management approach. This aligns with the safetyist view that AI's complexity creates novel, often hidden, attack surfaces and systemic vulnerabilities.
key_points.verbatim: AI systems can also present new risks to privacy by allowing inference to identify individuals or previously private information about individuals.

key_points.point: The document warns that measurement approaches can be oversimplified, gamed, or lack critical nuance, leading to reliance on metrics that fail to account for real-world contexts. This reflects the safetyist concern that optimizing for narrow, easily measurable metrics can undermine human values and lead to unexpected, harmful outcomes. It advocates for continual improvement and re-evaluation of metrics to avoid these pitfalls.
key_points.verbatim: Measurement approaches can be oversimplified, gamed, lack critical nuance, become used and relied upon in unexpected ways, fail to account for differences in affected groups and contexts.

key_points.point: The document advocates for rigorous, ongoing monitoring and documentation of AI systems to ensure they remain safe and aligned with organizational values. It emphasizes that risk management must be an iterative process that adapts to emergent risks in real-world deployment. This approach prioritizes proactive oversight and accountability mechanisms to prevent catastrophic or systemic failures.
key_points.verbatim: Approaches, personnel, and documentation are in place to regularly identify and track existing, unanticipated, and emergent AI risks based on factors such as intended and actual performance in deployed contexts.

key_points.point: The document promotes the integration of human feedback and participatory engagement to identify risks that automated metrics might miss. By involving end users and impacted communities, organizations can better understand the real-world impacts of AI systems. This strategy aims to bridge the gap between technical performance metrics and actual human-centric safety.
key_points.verbatim: Assessing impact is a two-way effort. Many AI system outcomes and impacts may not be visible or recognizable to AI actors across the development and deployment dimensions of the AI lifecycle, and may require direct feedback about system outcomes from the perspective of end users and impacted groups.

key_points.point: The document acknowledges that AI systems can cause disparate impacts and exacerbate existing social inequalities, such as the digital divide. It highlights that failure to address these design issues leads to measurable legal and ethical risks. This aligns with the skeptic focus on the immediate, tangible harms AI poses to marginalized groups.
key_points.verbatim: Disparate impact is broadly defined as a facially neutral policy or practice that disproportionately harms a group based on a protected trait. ... Such factors may mean different communities experience bias or other negative impacts when trying to access AI systems.

key_points.point: The document suggests that organizations must maintain policies for training staff and documenting regulatory compliance to mitigate risks. It emphasizes that risk management is not just technical but requires clear chains of command and accountability. This aligns with the skeptic view that AI risks are manageable through rigorous, human-centered organizational processes and data quality standards.
key_points.verbatim: Lack of clear information about responsibilities and chains of command will limit the effectiveness of risk management.

key_points.point: The document advocates for the inclusion of diverse, multidisciplinary teams—including civil liberties and ethics experts—throughout the AI lifecycle to mitigate bias and discrimination. This participatory approach aims to ensure that AI systems do not disproportionately harm vulnerable communities or perpetuate existing societal inequities.
key_points.verbatim: Entities include diverse perspectives from technical and non-technical communities throughout the AI life cycle to anticipate and mitigate unintended consequences including potential bias and discrimination.

key_points.point: The document suggests establishing mechanisms for impacted individuals to contest problematic AI outcomes and provide feedback on negative impacts. This creates a form of civil rights guardrail, allowing for public recourse against automated decisions that may violate individual rights or cause harm.
key_points.verbatim: Establish mechanisms to provide recourse for impacted individuals or communities to contest problematic AI system outcomes.

key_points.point: The document acknowledges that AI systems are dynamic and can perform in unexpected ways, challenging traditional governance structures. It highlights the need for continuous monitoring and incident response to address the inherent unpredictability and potential for harm in deployed AI systems.
key_points.verbatim: AI systems are dynamic and may perform in unexpected ways once deployed or after deployment. Continuous monitoring is a risk management process for tracking unexpected issues and performance changes, in real-time or at a specific frequency, across the AI system lifecycle.

key_points.point: The document suggests that organizations should formally weigh an AI system's negative risks against its benefits to determine if it is an appropriate solution. This 'risk-utility' approach acknowledges that AI may not always be the right tool for a task. It aligns with the skeptic focus on practical, measurable outcomes over blind adoption.
key_points.verbatim: A standard risk management practice is to formally weigh an AI system's negative risks against its benefits, and to determine if the AI system is an appropriate solution.

key_points.point: The document encourages organizations to document and share information about near-misses and incidents to avoid repeating past failures. This focus on learning from real-world errors is a hallmark of the skeptic approach to risk management. It prioritizes fixing observable problems over speculative future risks.
key_points.verbatim: Are processes for operator reporting of incidents and near-misses documented and available?

key_points.point: The document emphasizes the necessity of participatory auditing and feedback loops involving end users and impacted groups. By requiring organizations to capture feedback during deployment, it seeks to uncover negative impacts that are not visible through internal testing alone.
key_points.verbatim: Establish mechanisms to capture feedback from system end users and potentially impacted groups while system is in deployment.

key_points.point: The document supports a risk-utility approach to AI deployment, where organizations must weigh the potential value of an AI system against its negative impacts. It explicitly suggests that organizations should be prepared to decommission systems that fail to meet safety or ethical standards.
key_points.verbatim: Transparent monitoring and managing residual risks enables cost benefit analysis and the examination of potential values of AI systems versus its potential negative impacts.

key_points.point: The document advocates for participatory auditing and the inclusion of diverse, interdisciplinary teams to identify risks and biases. It emphasizes that organizations must engage with community groups and stakeholders to understand the real-world impacts of AI, reflecting the skeptic focus on measurable, human-centered harm mitigation.
key_points.verbatim: Successfully mapping context requires a team of AI actors with a diversity of experience, expertise, abilities and backgrounds, and with the resources and independence to engage in critical inquiry.

key_points.point: The document suggests that organizations should consider non-AI alternatives when the risks of an AI system outweigh its benefits or when the context is too complex to manage safely. This aligns with the skeptic view that AI is not always the appropriate solution and that its deployment should be constrained by civil rights and societal norms.
key_points.verbatim: Context mapping also includes discussion and consideration of non-AI or non-technology alternatives especially as related to whether the given context is narrow enough to manage AI and its potential negative impacts.

key_points.point: The document highlights that AI systems fundamentally challenge existing legal and organizational frameworks, necessitating a shift toward socio-technical metrics. It argues that organizations must evaluate AI performance not just on accuracy, but on alignment with societal values and legal requirements.
key_points.verbatim: Review the documented system purpose from a socio-technical perspective and in consideration of societal values.

key_points.point: The document advocates for pragmatic, evidence-based risk management by requiring organizations to document 'off-label' uses and analyze tradeoffs across trustworthiness characteristics. This reflects a skeptic focus on managing the tangible, present-day risks of AI deployment rather than speculative future scenarios. It emphasizes that risk management must be an ongoing, documented process rather than a one-time check.
key_points.verbatim: Review uses of AI systems for â€œoff-labelâ€  purposes, especially in settings that organizations have deemed as high-risk. Document decisions, risk-related trade-offs, and system limitations.

key_points.point: The document promotes participatory auditing by suggesting that organizations include impacted communities, civil society, and external experts in the formulation of AI priorities and impact assessments. This aligns with the skeptic desire to democratize AI oversight and ensure that systems are not designed solely by and for the benefit of the deploying entity.
key_points.verbatim: Include potentially impacted groups, communities and external entities (e.g. civil society organizations, research institutes, local community groups, and trade associations) in the formulation of priorities, definitions and outcomes during impact assessment activities.

key_points.point: The document acknowledges that data used in AI systems is often selected based on convenience rather than suitability, leading to datasets that are not representative of the populations they model. It highlights that this practice introduces systemic bias and risks, reinforcing the skeptic belief that AI systems often perpetuate or exacerbate existing societal inequalities.
key_points.verbatim: The difficulty of finding the â€œrightâ€  data may lead AI actors to select datasets based more on accessibility and availability than on suitability for operationalizing the phenomenon that the AI system intends to support or inform.

key_points.point: The document strongly advocates for participatory approaches, requiring organizations to engage with potentially affected groups and communities. It suggests that these stakeholders provide essential input on system benefits and limitations. This aligns with the skeptic focus on democratizing AI development and ensuring accountability to those impacted by the technology.
key_points.verbatim: It is encouraged that risk management and assessment of benefits and impacts include processes for regular and meaningful communication with potentially affected groups and communities. These stakeholders can provide valuable input related to systemsâ€™ benefits and possible limitations.

key_points.point: The document highlights the critical need for documentation regarding AI system purpose, utility, and potential risks. It suggests that organizations should maintain awareness of stakeholders and document the rationale behind deployment decisions. This addresses the skeptic concern that lack of transparency and documentation leads to systems that are difficult to audit or maintain.
key_points.verbatim: Organizations are encouraged to define and document system purpose and utility, and its potential positive impacts and benefits beyond current known performance benchmarks. Maintain awareness and documentation of the individuals, groups, or communities who make up the systemâ€™s internal and external stakeholders.

key_points.point: The document advocates for participatory auditing by engaging diverse stakeholder groups, including end-users and impacted communities, throughout the AI development pipeline. It argues that these groups often possess knowledge of benefits and harms that are invisible to the developers themselves. This approach aims to democratize the monitoring process and ensure that AI systems are evaluated against real-world social impacts rather than just technical benchmarks.
key_points.verbatim: After an AI system is deployed, engaging different stakeholder groups – who may be aware of, or experience, benefits or negative impacts that are unknown to AI actors involved in the design, development and deployment activities – allows organizations to understand and monitor system benefits and potential negative impacts more readily.

key_points.point: The document asserts that AI systems are inherently brittle and prone to failure modes that are not well-described or understood. It notes that these systems often fail to transfer well outside of their training environments, leading to significant risks in real-world deployment. This belief justifies the skeptic's demand for rigorous, context-specific testing and continuous monitoring of AI systems.
key_points.verbatim: The current AI systems are brittle, the failure modes are not well described, and the systems are dependent on the context in which they were developed and do not transfer well outside of the training environment.

key_points.point: The document proposes that organizations must establish clear, documented processes for identifying and reporting AI-related errors, incidents, and negative impacts. It suggests that metrics should be updated regularly to reflect the evolving nature of AI risks and the specific context of use. This focus on incident response and continuous improvement is a core skeptic strategy for managing the inevitable failures of AI technology.
key_points.verbatim: Document reports of errors, incidents and negative impacts and assess sufficiency and efficacy of existing metrics for repairs, and upgrades.

key_points.point: The document acknowledges that AI systems often fail to generalize to real-world settings, leading to inaccurate or unreliable outcomes. It highlights the danger of using proxies to measure complex social constructs like fairness or honesty, which can lead to undetected biases and systemic errors. This reflects a skeptical view of AI's inherent functionality and the risks of over-reliance on automated metrics.
key_points.verbatim: Validation risks include the use of proxies or other indicators that are often constructed by AI development teams to operationalize phenomena that are either not directly observable or measurable (e.g, fairness, hireability, honesty, propensity to commit a crime).

key_points.point: The document suggests that AI systems should be subject to rigorous, factory-like reporting and incident tracking. It encourages organizations to maintain audit logs, report failures to incident databases, and share information about attack patterns. This aligns with the skeptic's desire to treat AI as a standard industrial technology that requires strict accountability and public oversight.
key_points.verbatim: Verify that information about errors and attack patterns is shared with incident databases, other organizations with similar systems, and system users and stakeholders.

key_points.point: The document acknowledges that bias is not just a technical error but can be systemic, computational, or human-cognitive, and that it can become ingrained in automated systems. It notes that even systems with mitigated biases may still exacerbate existing disparities or be inaccessible to certain groups. This aligns with the skeptic view that AI often reinforces existing societal inequalities rather than solving them.
key_points.verbatim: Bias exists in many forms and can become ingrained in the automated systems that help make decisions about our lives. While bias is not always a negative phenomenon, AI systems can potentially increase the speed and scale of biases and perpetuate and amplify harms to individuals, groups, communities, organizations, and society.

key_points.point: The document highlights the environmental costs of AI, including energy and water consumption, greenhouse gas emissions, and the lifecycle impacts of hardware production and electronic waste. It explicitly mentions 'rebound effects' where efficiency gains are offset by increased consumption. This supports the skeptic focus on the measurable, negative externalities of AI deployment.
key_points.verbatim: Indirect negative impacts to the environment reflect the complexity of interactions between human behavior, socio-economic systems, and the environment and can include induced consumption and “rebound effects”, where efficiency gains are offset by accelerated resource consumption.

key_points.point: The document advocates for practical, context-specific fairness assessments that involve direct engagement with impacted communities. It suggests moving beyond general metrics to identify specific harms like stereotyping or erasure. This aligns with the skeptic intention to focus on real-world, measurable harms rather than abstract or purely technical definitions of AI performance.
key_points.verbatim: Conduct fairness assessments to manage computational and statistical forms of bias which include the following steps: Identify types of harms, including allocational, representational, quality of service, stereotyping, or erasure.

key_points.point: The document highlights the limitations of relying solely on quantitative metrics for AI evaluation, suggesting that these metrics often fail to capture the full scope of social harm or bias. It encourages organizations to look beyond simple performance logs and incorporate qualitative feedback from those affected by the technology. This reflects a skepticism toward purely technical or automated approaches to AI governance.
key_points.verbatim: Many AI system outcomes and impacts may not be visible or recognizable to AI actors across the development and deployment dimensions of the AI lifecycle, and may require direct feedback about system outcomes from the perspective of end users and impacted groups.

key_points.point: The document acknowledges that AI systems can produce harmful outcomes that are not immediately apparent to developers, such as discrimination or usability failures. It emphasizes the necessity of establishing recourse mechanisms and bug bounties to address these real-world harms. This aligns with the skeptic view that AI systems are prone to immediate, measurable failures that require active, human-led intervention.
key_points.verbatim: Risks identified in the Map function may be complex, emerge over time, or difficult to measure. Systematic methods for risk tracking, including novel measurement approaches, can be established as part of regular monitoring and improvement processes.
